extracted.intended_audience: readers of historical fiction / writers crafting medieval scenes
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding considerations and implicit standards for portraying medieval religious and social scenes — how to render speech, persuasion, authority, and local politics convincingly in historical fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vernacular language yields immediacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The text argues that reading the gospels 'in the English tongue' gave the words 'a new life and meaning' and made them 'the property of the listener as they could never be when a dead language was used as the medium of expression.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the vernacular to make familiar material feel immediate and personally owned by characters/audience; contrast the dead/formal register with lively native speech to show emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural eloquence beats studied artifice
rubrics_metrics.description: Edred is struck by 'the eloquence of one of nature's orators that carries away the heart far more than the studied oratory which is the result of practice and artifice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray conviction and earnestness (gestures, confidence, lack of hesitation) to make a speaker persuasive; show natural passion rather than polished, rehearsed rhetoric for emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address audience needs (supply what is sought)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator notes the people were 'fairly starving for want of spiritual food' and therefore eagerly gathered round any who would teach them of the Saviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting public speech or teaching, make clear how the speaker meets an unmet need in the audience — hunger/longing explains receptivity and tension between official ritual and popular desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct reading can be more faithful than spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator contrasts the 'miracle play' with the hunchback's reading, saying the play was 'half comical, half blasphemous' and that the gospel could be brought home 'so far more faithfully and eloquently by simply reading the gospel words in the tongue of the common people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrasts (theatre vs plain reading) to evaluate authenticity: sometimes simple, literal presentation of source material is truer to its spirit than elaborate or artificial dramatization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Untrained interpretation risks error and irreverence
rubrics_metrics.description: Brother Emmanuel warns that 'the reading and expounding of the Scriptures by the ignorant and unlearned led almost invariably to those other sins of blasphemy and irreverence which curdled the very blood in his veins.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If depicting lay or populist exegesis, show plausible consequences and tensions (misunderstanding, doctrinal drift, accusations of blasphemy) to justify conflict and the responses of authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obedience to ecclesiastical authority as moral standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The monk teaches that 'the first sin... was the sin of disobedience' and insists there are 'certain things hidden, only to be revealed ... through the ordinances of the Church,' implying obedience is a virtue and curiosity can be sinful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing clerical characters or moral debates, present obedience and submission to institutional authority as a coherent moral position (with motives, internal logic, and rhetoric), not merely as repression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence about public alignment with controversial causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Warbel and Sir Oliver worry that to 'appear to side with those against whom the foul charge of heresy is brought' is 'dangerous work' and may bring retaliation from powerful enemies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show characters weighing the risks of visible support for unpopular figures; dramatize prudence, fear of political reprisal, and calculations of reputation and safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political diplomacy and patronage matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The prior is described as 'the most powerful man in the county' whose favor can prevent persecution; Sir Oliver values keeping the prior as an ally and paying sums to secure indulgence and protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict social power networks, clientage, and the transactional nature of protection (gifts, payments, neutral mediation) to render medieval politics believable and to provide plot levers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penance, confession, and ecclesiastical remedies as narrative mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Edred seeks confession and is given 'heavy penance' and the narrative describes paying sums for indulgence as a way to 'purchase this indulgence' and avert trouble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use institutional rituals (confession, penance, indulgences) both to reveal inner conflict and to advance plot (penance as imposed restraint, payment as political solution). Describe their social and psychological effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible preaching must reinforce sacramental order
rubrics_metrics.description: Brother Emmanuel longs to preach so that 'all might have news of the Son of God, yet might be taught to revere the holy sacraments more rather than less... and to respect the priesthood,' showing a model of preaching that both evangelizes and upholds ecclesiastical structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying reformist or evangelical impulses, show how a character might balance outreach with deference to existing institutions — this tension can humanize clerical reformers and complicate conflicts.
